overview: Both sterilize using heat, but moist versus dry heat changes what materials each can safely and effectively be used on.

aspects.label: Principle
aspects.valueA: Moist heat under pressure — saturated steam denatures and coagulates microbial proteins efficiently at lower temperatures than dry heat.
aspects.valueB: Dry heat — oxidation of cell constituents and protein denaturation at higher temperatures and longer exposure times than moist heat.

aspects.label: Mechanism
aspects.valueA: Pressurized steam penetrates materials and transfers heat rapidly via condensation.
aspects.valueB: Hot air circulates around items; heat transfer is slower since air conducts heat less efficiently than steam.

aspects.label: Temperature / Pressure
aspects.valueA: A commonly cited standard cycle is 121°C at about 15 psi for 15–20 minutes for a typical liquid/instrument load — exact parameters vary by load type and validated protocol.
aspects.valueB: A commonly cited standard cycle is 160–180°C for 1–2 hours depending on the specific protocol and load — exact parameters vary by manufacturer/standard.

aspects.label: Equipment
aspects.valueA: Pressure vessel with a steam generator, gauge, and safety valve.
aspects.valueB: Insulated chamber with electrical heating elements and (often) a fan for air circulation.

aspects.label: Duration
aspects.valueA: Shorter cycles overall due to more efficient heat transfer via steam.
aspects.valueB: Longer cycles overall since dry air transfers heat less efficiently than steam.

aspects.label: Applications
aspects.valueA: Culture media, aqueous solutions, surgical instruments, and other heat-and-moisture-tolerant items.
aspects.valueB: Glassware, metal instruments, oils, powders, and other items that must stay dry or would be damaged by moisture.

aspects.label: Safety
aspects.valueA: Pressurized system — requires correct venting/cool-down before opening to avoid burns or injury.
aspects.valueB: High surface and chamber temperatures — requires appropriate handling precautions to avoid burns.

aspects.label: Limitations / Pitfalls
aspects.valueA: Not suitable for materials damaged by moisture or pressure (e.g. some plastics, powders, oils).
aspects.valueB: Less efficient than steam for the same temperature; not suitable for materials that degrade at high dry heat or for liquids.

aspects.label: Key Distinguishing Feature
aspects.valueA: Uses moist heat (steam under pressure) for faster sterilization at lower temperatures.
aspects.valueB: Uses dry heat for materials that must remain moisture-free.

aspects.label: Primary Purpose / Indication
aspects.valueA: Sterilizing moisture-tolerant items and liquids efficiently.
aspects.valueB: Sterilizing moisture-sensitive items that can tolerate prolonged high dry heat.

overlay.examHighYieldNote: Autoclave = steam, faster, lower temp. Hot air oven = dry, slower, higher temp.
overlay.memoryTrick: "Steam works fast because it's wet. Dry heat is slow because it's shy about moisture."
overlay.choiceRule: If the item can get wet, autoclave it. If it must stay dry (powders, oils, some glassware), use the hot air oven.
